warmup.q: A fixed pool of 4 threads has 10 queued tasks that take 1 second each. main calls pool.shutdown() and then prints "done". When does "done" appear?
options: Right away, while the tasks keep running
After about 3 seconds, when the last task finishes
Never, because shutdown() blocks until someone calls awaitTermination()
Right away, and the 10 tasks are cancelled
warmup.why: shutdown() only stops new submissions. Queued and running tasks carry on, and the call returns at once. Waiting is a separate step: awaitTermination or, since JDK 19, close(). Nothing is cancelled; that would be shutdownNow().

sections.h: A thread per task costs time and has no ceiling
sections.html:
Here is a measurement from ThreadPerTaskDemo below. Five thousand tiny tasks, each run on a brand-new thread, took between 0.5 and 1.5 seconds per round on a 4-core machine, depending on how busy it was. The same tasks on a pool of four reused threads took 6 to 25 ms.

The work was identical. The difference is the threads. A Java platform thread wraps an operating system thread. Starting one means a system call, a new stack (on 64-bit Linux the JVM reserves 1 MB of address space per thread by default) and registration with the OS scheduler. When the thread ends, all of that is torn down again. For a task that runs for microseconds, the setup costs far more than the work.

The second cost is worse, because it only shows up under load. Thread-per-task has no upper limit. If 3,000 authorization requests arrive at once, you get 3,000 threads. Something runs out first: the process thread limit, memory for stacks, or CPU time spent switching between threads that all want to run. In Java the first sign is often java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread, during your busiest hour.

A thread pool fixes both problems. It creates a few threads once and keeps them. Each thread loops: take a task from a queue, run it, take the next one. The pool size caps how many tasks run at the same time, and the rest wait in the queue.

Virtual threads, the subject of the "Virtual threads" track, make threads cheap to create, so the first cost mostly goes away for them. The second one does not. You still need a limit on how much work runs at once; with virtual threads you put that limit on the scarce resource instead of on the threads.

try.title: Pay for 5,000 threads
steps: Predict first: for 5,000 tiny tasks, how many times slower is one new thread per task than a pool of 4? Twice? Ten times? A hundred?
Run ThreadPerTaskDemo (Java or Kotlin, they do the same thing) with the command below. It runs two rounds.
Run it again with -Pargs=10000 added. Does each column double?

code.title: ThreadPerTaskDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ public class ThreadPerTaskDemo { static final LongAdder work = new LongAdder(); static void task() { work.add(Long.toHexString(System.nanoTime()).length()); // a few nanoseconds of real work } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 5_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 2; round++) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task long t0 = System.nanoTime(); CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) { new Thread(() -> { task(); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); long perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.execute(ThreadPerTaskDemo::task); } // close() waits for all of them long pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms%n", round, tasks, perTask, pooled); } } }

alt.title: ThreadPerTaskDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder private val work = LongAdder() private fun task() { work.add(System.nanoTime().toString(16).length.toLong()) // a few nanoseconds of real work } /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tasks = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 5_000 for (round in 1..2) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task var t0 = System.nanoTime() val done = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { Thread { task(); done.countDown() }.start() } done.await() val perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> repeat(tasks) { pool.execute(::task) } } // close() waits for all of them val pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms".format(round, tasks, perTask, pooled)) } }

try.expect: On the machine this was written on, one thread per task took 0.5 to 1.5 seconds per round and the pool took 6 to 25 ms: 50 to 150 times faster. The pool's first round is the slowest because the JIT is still warming up. With 10,000 tasks the thread-per-task column roughly doubles, because the cost is paid per thread. The pool pays it four times in total.

sections.h: Executor runs tasks, ExecutorService owns the threads
sections.html:
java.util.concurrent splits the idea into two interfaces.

Executor has one method, void execute(Runnable task). It says nothing about threads. An implementation may run the task on the calling thread, on a new thread or on a pool, and code that takes an Executor doesn't care which.

ExecutorService extends it with what a pool needs: submit (which returns a Future, a handle you can use to wait for the task's result), invokeAll and invokeAny, and the lifecycle methods shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination and, since JDK 19, close. You rarely implement it. You get one from the Executors factory:

Java
ExecutorService fixed  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);          // 8 threads, unbounded queue
ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();      // 1 thread, tasks run in order
ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();          // grows without limit, idle threads die after 60 s
ExecutorService vts    = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task
Kotlin
val fixed  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)              // 8 threads, unbounded queue
val single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()          // 1 thread, tasks run in order
val cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()              // grows without limit, idle threads die after 60 s
val vts    = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()  // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task

The first three are built on ThreadPoolExecutor with different settings. Lesson 2 of this track takes it apart.

Now the trap. execute and submit look interchangeable, and they handle failure in opposite ways. Here is what SwallowDemo prints for the same failing task sent both ways:

--- execute ---
charging on pool-1-thread-1
Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-1" java.lang.IllegalStateException: card issuer returned 502
--- submit ---
charging on pool-1-thread-2
submit: nothing printed. isDone=true

With execute, the exception escapes the task and kills the worker thread. The thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler prints the stack trace (that is the default handler's job), and the pool starts a replacement worker. That is why the second task runs on pool-1-thread-2.

With submit, the pool wraps your task in a FutureTask, which catches the exception and stores it in the Future. Nothing is printed. The only way to see the failure is to call get(), which throws ExecutionException with your exception as its cause. If nobody calls get(), the failure is gone.

So choose on purpose. Use execute for fire-and-forget work, so failures at least reach the handler. Use submit only when some code will call get(). Lesson 9 of this track shows how to log failures from both.

try.title: Lose an exception on purpose
steps: Run SwallowDemo below and read the thread name printed for each run.
Delete the whole --- get --- part (the println and the try block around f.get()). Predict: will any trace of the second failure remain?

code.title: SwallowDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ public class SwallowDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Runnable charge = () -> { System.out.println("charging on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); throw new IllegalStateException("card issuer returned 502"); }; System.out.println("--- execute ---"); pool.execute(charge); Thread.sleep(200); // give the stack trace time to print System.out.println("--- submit ---"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(charge); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone()); System.out.println("--- get ---"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } } }

alt.title: SwallowDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> val charge = Runnable { println("charging on " + Thread.currentThread().name) throw IllegalStateException("card issuer returned 502") } println("--- execute ---") pool.execute(charge) Thread.sleep(200) // give the stack trace time to print println("--- submit ---") val f = pool.submit(charge) Thread.sleep(200) println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone) println("--- get ---") try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.cause) } } }

try.expect: The first run prints a stack trace for the execute failure, then the submit task runs on pool-1-thread-2 because the first worker died. The get() block prints the ExecutionException and its cause. Without that block, the second failure leaves no trace at all: the exception sits inside a Future nobody reads.

sections.h: shutdown() starts the stop, awaitTermination() waits for it
sections.html:
An ExecutorService moves one way: running, then shutting down (or stopping), then terminated. Two methods start that trip, and neither of them waits.

shutdown() closes the door. New tasks are rejected with RejectedExecutionException. Queued tasks and running tasks carry on. The method returns at once.

shutdownNow() closes the door and empties the room. It removes every queued task that has not started and returns them as a List<Runnable>. Then it interrupts the threads that are running tasks. An interrupt is a request, not a kill. A task blocked in sleep, wait or BlockingQueue.take wakes up with an InterruptedException. A task in a CPU loop that never checks the flag keeps running. Lesson 4 of this track covers that protocol.

To wait for the end, call awaitTermination(timeout, unit). It returns true if the pool terminated in time and false if not. Together they make the shutdown idiom from the ExecutorService Javadoc (the timeouts are yours to pick):

Java
pool.shutdown();                                         // 1. no new work
try {
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {  // 2. let the backlog finish
        pool.shutdownNow();                              // 3. interrupt the stragglers
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS))
            log.error("pool did not terminate");
    }
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    pool.shutdownNow();                                  // we were interrupted: stop now
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();                  // and keep the flag for our caller
}
Kotlin
pool.shutdown()                                          // 1. no new work
try {
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {  // 2. let the backlog finish
        pool.shutdownNow()                               // 3. interrupt the stragglers
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS))
            log.error("pool did not terminate")
    }
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    pool.shutdownNow()                                   // we were interrupted: stop now
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt()                   // and keep the flag for our caller
}

Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources can do the waiting. close() calls shutdown() and waits until every task has finished. If the waiting thread is interrupted, it calls shutdownNow(), keeps waiting, and sets the interrupt flag again before it returns. There is no timeout, so close() blocks forever on a task that never ends. Use close() for a short-lived pool inside one method. Use the idiom for a long-lived pool that must stop within a deadline.

Forget both and you get a different bug. The threads of newFixedThreadPool are not daemon threads, so they keep the JVM alive after main returns, waiting for tasks that will never come.

try.title: Watch shutdown not wait
steps: ShutdownDemo queues six 300 ms settlement batches on two threads, then calls shutdown(). Predict the timestamp on the shutdown returned line, then run it.
Run it again with -Pargs=now, which calls shutdownNow() after 100 ms instead. Predict how many batches settle.

code.title: ShutdownDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a pool of 2 threads with 6 queued 300 ms tasks. */ public class ShutdownDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static Runnable settle(int id) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); // a 300 ms call to the ledger log("settled batch " + id); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("batch " + id + " interrupted"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean now = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("now"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) pool.execute(settle(i)); if (now) { Thread.sleep(100); List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); log("shutdownNow returned " + neverStarted.size() + " tasks that never started"); } else { pool.shutdown(); log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=" + pool.isShutdown() + " isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } try { pool.execute(settle(7)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { log("batch 7 rejected: the pool is shut down"); } boolean done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); log("awaitTermination returned " + done + ". isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } }

alt.title: ShutdownDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun settle(id: Int) = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(300) // a 300 ms call to the ledger log("settled batch $id") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("batch $id interrupted") Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a pool of 2 threads with 6 queued 300 ms tasks. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val now = args.firstOrNull() == "now" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2) for (i in 1..6) pool.execute(settle(i)) if (now) { Thread.sleep(100) val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() log("shutdownNow returned ${neverStarted.size} tasks that never started") } else { pool.shutdown() log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=${pool.isShutdown} isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") } try { pool.execute(settle(7)) } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { log("batch 7 rejected: the pool is shut down") } val done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) log("awaitTermination returned $done. isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") }

try.expect: With shutdown(), that line prints within a few milliseconds, batch 7 is rejected, and the six batches settle in pairs at about 300, 600 and 900 ms. Only then does awaitTermination return true. With now, batches 1 and 2 are interrupted in their sleep, shutdownNow hands back the 4 batches that never started, nothing settles, and the pool terminates at about 100 ms.

sections.h: A pool is a queue and a few threads that loop
sections.html:
Strip away the options and a fixed pool is small enough to write in a lab. Each worker thread runs this loop:

Java
while (true) {
    Runnable task = queue.take();   // blocks while the queue is empty
    if (task == POISON) return;     // shutdown: time to exit
    task.run();
}
Kotlin
while (true) {
    val task = queue.take()          // blocks while the queue is empty
    if (task === POISON) return      // shutdown: time to exit
    task.run()
}

execute puts the task on a BlockingQueue, and workers take it off. The queue does the hand-off between threads, and the number of workers is the limit on how many tasks run at once.

Shutdown is the interesting part. Idle workers are blocked inside take(), so the pool has to wake them. One way is a poison pill: a marker task, one per worker, added behind every real task. A worker that takes a pill exits. The queue is first in, first out, so every task submitted before shutdown() runs before any worker sees a pill. shutdownNow() drains the queue instead, adds fresh pills, and interrupts the workers, so idle ones fall out of take() and busy ones get the request to stop.

There is one race to get right, and it is the check-then-act shape from "Race conditions: why count++ lies". execute checks the shutdown flag, then queues the task. If shutdown() runs between those two steps, the task lands behind the pills and never runs, although the caller was told it was accepted. So both methods take the same lock, and the check and the queueing happen as one step.

ThreadPoolExecutor solves the same problem with one AtomicInteger called ctl. It packs the run state into the top 3 bits and the worker count into the other 29, so a single compare-and-set can check and change both. The lab uses a plain lock instead. It is slower and much easier to read, which is the right trade when the goal is to see the moving parts.

Check yourself: in the toy pool, shutdown() adds one pill instead of one per worker, and the pool has four workers. What happens? One worker takes the pill and exits. The other three stay blocked in take() forever, so awaitTermination returns false. They are not daemon threads, so the JVM never exits either.

analogy: A pool is a courier office. The couriers are the threads, hired once and kept. Parcels go into one in-tray (the queue), and whichever courier is free takes the next one. shutdown() is the sign on the door that says "no more parcels": the couriers still clear the tray. shutdownNow() hands the tray back to the customers and phones every courier on the road to come back. The analogy breaks at that phone call. A real courier hears it. A Java task hears an interrupt only if it checks for one or is blocked in a method that does.
world: A Kafka consumer in a payment service often hands records to a fixed pool so slow ledger writes don't stall polling. When Kubernetes stops the pod, it sends SIGTERM and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds by default) before SIGKILL. That is your shutdown budget. Stop polling first, then shutdown() the pool, awaitTermination for about 20 seconds, then shutdownNow() and log what it handed back, and commit offsets only for records that finished. Quarkus manages its own worker pool, and a Temporal WorkerFactory stops its threads when you shut the factory down. The pools you create yourself, for a fan-out to card issuers or a nightly settlement job, are yours to close.
mistake: Calling shutdown() and treating the work as done. A settlement job runs pool.shutdown(); dataSource.close(); and the batches still running fail with connection errors. The name sounds final and the call returns quickly, so it reads like a wait. It only stops new submissions. Wait with awaitTermination (or close() on JDK 19 and later) before you release anything the tasks still use.

compare.title: Closing a pool in Java and Kotlin

java.title: UseDemo.java (sketch)
java.html: try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (int n = 1; n <= 10; n++) { int k = n; futures.add(pool.submit(() -> k * k)); } int total = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : futures) { total += f.get(); // must handle InterruptedException and ExecutionException } System.out.println("sum of squares 1..10 = " + total); } // close(): shutdown, then wait for every task

kotlin.title: UseDemo.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Kotlin's use {} calls ExecutorService.close() (JDK 19+), which waits for the tasks to finish. */ fun main() { val total = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> val futures = (1..10).map { n -> pool.submit<Int> { n * n } } futures.sumOf { it.get() } // get() can still throw ExecutionException; Kotlin just doesn't force a catch } println("sum of squares 1..10 = $total") }

compare.note: Both versions end in ExecutorService.close(), so the waiting is the same. Kotlin's use is its try-with-resources, and it works on a pool because ExecutorService has been AutoCloseable since JDK 19 (on older JDKs, write the shutdown idiom in a finally). The real difference is checked exceptions. Java makes you deal with InterruptedException and ExecutionException from get(). Kotlin compiles without a catch, so a failed task surfaces as an exception you never planned for. If you later wrap a pool for coroutines with asCoroutineDispatcher(), the dispatcher needs closing too; closing it shuts the pool down.

worked.title: Stop a settlement job without losing batches

steps.say: A nightly job settles merchant batches on a pool of 4. Here is the end of main as first written. Decide what happens to batches still running when this code reaches dataSource.close().
steps.code: for (Batch b : batches) pool.execute(() -> settle(b)); pool.shutdown(); dataSource.close(); // release the 20 DB connections log.info("settlement finished");

alt.html: for (b in batches) pool.execute { settle(b) } pool.shutdown() dataSource.close() // release the 20 DB connections log.info("settlement finished")

steps.say: shutdown() returned at once. The log line lies, and dataSource.close() pulls connections away from batches that are still running, so they fail with connection errors. Nothing waited for anything.
Wait, with a deadline. The job has a 10 minute slot, so give the backlog 9 of them, then interrupt and record what never started. Release shared resources only after the pool has terminated.
steps.code: pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new batches try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish List<Runnable> unstarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt, collect the rest log.warn("{} batches never started", unstarted.size()); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } dataSource.close(); // 4. only now

alt.html: pool.shutdown() // 1. no new batches try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish val unstarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt, collect the rest log.warn("{} batches never started", unstarted.size) pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } dataSource.close() // 4. only now

steps.say: If the job has no deadline, JDK 19's try-with-resources is shorter, and the order is right by construction: the block cannot end before the pool has terminated.
steps.code: try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (Batch b : batches) pool.execute(() -> settle(b)); } // close() waits for every batch dataSource.close(); log.info("settlement finished");

alt.html: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> for (b in batches) pool.execute { settle(b) } } // close() waits for every batch dataSource.close() log.info("settlement finished")

lab.title: Build a tiny fixed pool
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
Write execute: a null check, then, inside synchronized (lock), throw RejectedExecutionException if shutdown is set, otherwise queue.add(task).
Write workerLoop: take() a task, return on POISON or on InterruptedException, run the task, and count a RuntimeException in failed instead of letting it escape.
Write shutdown (under the lock: set the flag, add one POISON per worker) and awaitTermination (wait on the terminated latch).
Write shutdownNow: under the lock, set the flag, drain the queue into a list, remove the pills from it and add fresh ones. Then interrupt every worker and return the list.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them twice more.
hints: Why add pills in shutdownNow as well? A running task may swallow the interrupt. When it ends, its worker goes back to take(). Without a pill waiting there, that worker blocks forever and awaitTermination never returns true.
BlockingQueue.drainTo(list) moves everything in the queue into list in one call, in queue order.
The shutdownNow test checks that you return the very same Runnable objects, in the order they were queued. Don't wrap them.
lab.done: All eight tests in TinyPoolTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the shutdown idiom from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write static void stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace). It stops new work, waits up to grace for the backlog, interrupts stragglers, waits 5 more seconds, and handles its own interruption correctly. Then compare. Did you restore the interrupt flag?

answer.html: static void stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace) { pool.shutdown(); // no new tasks try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt what is still running if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { System.err.println("pool did not terminate"); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the flag for the caller } }

alt.title: stop.kt
alt.html: fun stop(pool: ExecutorService, grace: Duration) { pool.shutdown() // no new tasks try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { pool.shutdownNow() // interrupt what is still running if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { System.err.println("pool did not terminate") } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // keep the flag for the caller } }

recap: A new platform thread costs a system call and a stack, and thread-per-task has no limit. A pool reuses a few threads and queues the rest.
Executor is one method, execute. ExecutorService adds submit, invokeAll, invokeAny and the lifecycle.
execute lets a failure reach the UncaughtExceptionHandler. submit stores it in the Future, and you only see it if you call get().
shutdown() rejects new tasks and returns at once. shutdownNow() also interrupts running tasks and returns the ones that never started.
Wait with awaitTermination(timeout), or with close() and try-with-resources on JDK 19+, which waits with no timeout.
Inside, a fixed pool is a BlockingQueue plus worker threads that loop on take().

explain.prompt: A new teammate asks what shutdown(), shutdownNow() and awaitTermination() each do, and in what order the payments service should call them when the pod gets SIGTERM. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: shutdown() stops the pool from accepting new tasks but lets queued and running tasks finish. It returns immediately, so it is only the start. awaitTermination(timeout) is the waiting part: it blocks until the pool has finished everything or the timeout passes, and tells you which happened. shutdownNow() is the hard stop: it removes the tasks that never started, hands them back, and interrupts the running ones, which only works if those tasks respond to interrupts. On SIGTERM we have about 30 seconds. So: stop taking work from Kafka or HTTP first, call shutdown(), wait maybe 20 seconds with awaitTermination, then call shutdownNow() and log what came back, wait a few more seconds, and only then close the database pool.

deeper.html:
ThreadPoolExecutor has five run states, not three: RUNNING, SHUTDOWN, STOP, TIDYING and TERMINATED. shutdown() moves it to SHUTDOWN. shutdownNow() moves it to STOP, from either of the first two. When the queue is empty and the last worker has exited, the pool moves to TIDYING, runs the protected terminated() hook (override it to log or release something), and then becomes TERMINATED. Threads blocked in awaitTermination wake only at that last step.

The state and the worker count live together in one AtomicInteger called ctl. The top 3 bits hold the state and the low 29 bits hold the count. That is why the Javadoc caps a pool at about 500 million workers: (2^29) - 1. Packing both into one word lets execute check "still running?" and "room for one more worker?" and claim the slot with one compare-and-set, which is the same atomic check-and-act the lab gets from a lock.

One more detail from the Executors Javadoc: newSingleThreadExecutor() is "guaranteed not to be reconfigurable to use additional threads", unlike newFixedThreadPool(1). The fixed pool is a plain ThreadPoolExecutor, so any code holding it can cast it and call setMaximumPoolSize. The single-thread executor is wrapped so nobody can. If your design depends on tasks running one at a time, in order, say so with newSingleThreadExecutor().
